label: Phaedo · The Soul's Kinship
title: The Soul's Kinship
paragraphs: Good, he said.

Then, said Socrates, must we not ask ourselves something like this: to what kind of thing does it belong to suffer this, to be scattered, and for what kind of thing should we fear that it may suffer it, and for what kind not? And after that must we not consider in turn which of the two the soul is, and on that ground be confident or afraid for our own soul?
That's true, he said.

Now, does it belong to what has been put together and is composite by nature to suffer this, to be taken apart in the same way it was put together? And if there is anything that is in fact not composite, does it belong to that alone, if to anything, not to suffer it?
I think that's so, said Cebes.

Then the things that always stay the same and in the same condition are the ones most likely to be not composite, while the things that are now one way and now another and never the same are the composite ones?
I think so.

Then let us go, he said, to the same things we went to in the earlier argument. The reality itself, of whose being we give an account when we ask and when we answer: does it always stay in the same condition and the same, or is it now one way and now another? The equal itself, the beautiful itself, each thing itself that is, that which is: does it ever admit any change whatever? Or does each of them that is, being of one form, itself by itself, always stay in the same condition and the same, and never in any way or in any respect admit any alteration at all?
It must stay in the same condition and the same, Socrates, said Cebes.

And what about the many beautiful things, such as people or horses or cloaks or anything else whatever of that kind, or the many equal things, or all the things that have the same names as those? Do they stay the same? Or, quite the opposite of those, are they, so to speak, never in any way the same, either as themselves or as one another?
That again is so, said Cebes. They never stay in the same condition.

And these you could touch and see and perceive with the other senses, but the things that stay the same you could never lay hold of with anything other than the reasoning of the mind; such things are unseen and not visible?
That's entirely true, he said.
Then shall we set down, if you like, he said, two kinds of things that are, the visible and the unseen?
Let's set them down, he said.
And the unseen always stays the same, while the visible never stays the same?
Let's set that down too, he said.
Come then, he said, are we ourselves anything other than body on the one hand and soul on the other?
Nothing else, he said.
Which kind, then, would we say the body is more like and more akin to?
That's clear to everyone, he said: the visible.
And what about the soul? Is it visible or unseen?
Not visible to human beings, at least, Socrates, he said.
But surely we were speaking of what is visible and what is not to the nature of human beings. Or do you think it was to some other nature?
To that of human beings.
What do we say about the soul, then? That it is visible or invisible?
Not visible.
Unseen, then?
Yes.
Then soul is more like the unseen than body is, and body more like the visible.
It must be, by every necessity, Socrates.

And were we not also saying a while ago that the soul, when it uses the body as well to examine something, whether through sight or through hearing or through some other sense — for this is what examining through the body is, examining something through the senses — is then dragged by the body toward the things that never stay the same, and that it wanders and is confused and dizzy as if it were drunk, because it is in touch with things of that kind?
Certainly.

But when it examines by itself, it goes off there, to what is pure and always is and is immortal and stays in the same condition; and, being akin to this, it always stays with it, whenever it comes to be by itself and is allowed to. It has ceased from its wandering, and in the presence of those things it always stays the same and in the same condition, because it is in touch with things of that kind. And this state of the soul is called wisdom?
That's entirely well said and true, Socrates, he said.
Which kind, then, once more, do you think the soul is more like and more akin to, judging both from what was said before and from what is being said now?

I think, Socrates, he said, that after this line of inquiry everyone, even the slowest learner, would agree that soul is wholly and entirely more like what always stays in the same condition than what does not.
And the body?
More like the other.

Now look at it this way too. When soul and body are together, nature orders the one to be a slave and be ruled, and the other to rule and be master. By this again, which of the two do you think is like the divine and which like the mortal? Or do you not think that the divine is by nature such as to rule and lead, and the mortal such as to be ruled and be a slave?
I do.
Which, then, does the soul resemble?
Clearly, Socrates, the soul resembles the divine and the body the mortal.

Then consider, Cebes, he said, whether from all that has been said this is what follows for us: that soul is most like the divine and immortal and intelligible and of one form and indissoluble and what always stays in the same condition and the same as itself, while body in turn is most like the human and mortal and of many forms and not intelligible and dissoluble and what never stays the same as itself. Have we anything else to say against this, my dear Cebes, to show that it is not so?
We have not.
Well then, this being so, does it not belong to body to be quickly dissolved, and to soul in turn to be altogether indissoluble, or something close to that?
Of course.

You notice, then, he said, that when a person dies, the visible part of him, the body, which lies in the visible, the thing we call a corpse, to which it belongs to be dissolved and fall apart and be blown away, does not suffer any of this at once. It lasts for a fairly long time, and for a very long time indeed if someone dies with his body in fine condition and in a season as fine. For a body that has shrunk and been embalmed, like those embalmed in Egypt, stays almost whole for a time beyond reckoning; and some parts of the body, even if it rots, bones and sinews and everything of that kind, are still, so to speak, immortal. Is that not so?
Yes.

The soul, then, the unseen, which goes off to another place of that kind, noble and pure and unseen, to Hades, rightly so named, to the good and wise god, where, if the god is willing, my own soul too must shortly go — is this soul of ours, being such and of such a nature, blown apart and destroyed the moment it parts from the body, as most people say? Far from it, my dear Cebes and Simmias. Much rather it is like this. Suppose it parts pure, dragging nothing of the body along with it, because in life it had nothing to do with the body willingly, but shunned it and kept itself gathered into itself, because it always practiced this — and this is nothing other than practicing philosophy in the right way, and in truth practicing to die easily. Or would this not be the practice of dying?
Entirely so.

Then in that condition it goes away to what is like itself, the unseen, the divine and immortal and wise; and when it arrives there it is its lot to be happy, rid of wandering and folly and fears and wild loves and the other human evils, and, as is said of the initiated, truly spending the rest of time with the gods. Shall we say this, Cebes, or something else?
This, by Zeus, said Cebes.

But suppose, I think, that it parts from the body defiled and impure, because it was always with the body and tended it and loved it and was bewitched by it, by its desires and pleasures, so that it thinks nothing else is true except what is bodily, what one can touch and see and drink and eat and use for the pleasures of sex; while what is dark to the eyes and unseen, but intelligible and to be grasped by philosophy, this it has grown used to hating and trembling at and shunning. Do you think a soul in that condition will part from it itself by itself, unmixed?
Not in any way whatever, he said.
No, I think it will be shot through with the bodily, which its dealings and its company with the body, through being always with it and through much practice, have made part of its nature?
Certainly.

And this, my friend, we must think of as burdensome and heavy and earthy and visible. A soul of that kind, having this in it, is weighed down and dragged back into the visible place by fear of the unseen and of Hades, and, as is said, it roams among the monuments and the tombs, around which certain shadowy apparitions of souls have in fact been seen, the kind of images such souls produce, the ones that were not released pure but have a share of the visible, which is why they are seen.
That's likely, Socrates.

Likely indeed, Cebes; and likely too that these are not the souls of the good but those of the worthless, which are forced to wander around such places, paying the penalty for their former way of life, which was bad. And they wander until, through the desire of what follows along with them, the bodily, they are bound into a body again. And they are bound, as is likely, into characters of whatever kind they happen to have practiced in life.
What kinds do you mean, Socrates?

For example, those who have practiced gluttony and violence and drunkenness and have not guarded against them are likely to enter the races of donkeys and of animals like that. Or do you not think so?
What you say is very likely indeed.
And those who have honored injustice and tyranny and robbery above all, the races of wolves and hawks and kites. Or where else do we say such souls go?
No doubt, said Cebes, into such as those.
Then it is clear, he said, where each of the rest would go as well, according to the likeness of what they have practiced?
It is clear, he said. Of course.

Then the happiest even of these, he said, and the ones who go to the best place, are those who have pursued the popular and social virtue, which they call self-command and justice, and which has come from habit and practice without philosophy and intelligence?
In what way are these the happiest?
Because it is likely that they arrive back in a social and tame race of that kind, of bees perhaps or wasps or ants, or back in the very same human race, and that decent men are born from them.
Likely.

But to arrive at the race of gods is not permitted to anyone who has not practiced philosophy and does not depart entirely pure, but only to the lover of learning. It is for this, my friends Simmias and Cebes, that those who are philosophers in the right way keep away from all the desires of the body and hold firm and do not hand themselves over to them. It is not that they fear the ruin of their household and poverty, as the many and the lovers of money do; nor again is it from dread of the dishonor and ill repute of wickedness, like the lovers of power and the lovers of honor, that they keep away from them.
No, that wouldn't suit them, Socrates, said Cebes.

By Zeus, it would not, he said. And so, Cebes, those who care at all for their own soul, and do not live molding the body, say goodbye to all these people and do not travel the same road with them, since those people do not know where they are going. They themselves hold that one must not act against philosophy and the release and purification it brings, and so they turn this way, following philosophy where it leads.
How, Socrates?

I will tell you, he said. The lovers of learning know, he said, that when philosophy takes their soul in hand, the soul is simply bound fast in the body and glued to it, forced to examine the things that are through the body as through a prison, and not itself through itself, and wallowing in every kind of ignorance. And philosophy sees that the terrible thing about the prison is that it works through desire, so that the prisoner himself is the chief accomplice in his own imprisonment. As I say, then, the lovers of learning know that philosophy, taking their soul in hand in this condition, gently encourages it and tries to release it. It shows the soul that examination through the eyes is full of deceit, and so is examination through the ears and the other senses. It persuades the soul to withdraw from these, except so far as it must use them, and urges it to collect and gather itself into itself, and to trust nothing else but itself, whatever it thinks, itself by itself, of any of the things that are, itself by itself; and whatever it examines through other means, a thing that is different in different things, to hold none of that true. And it shows that what is of that kind is perceptible and visible, while what the soul itself sees is intelligible and unseen.

So the soul of the one who is truly a philosopher, thinking that it must not oppose this release, keeps away from pleasures and desires and pains as far as it can. It reckons that when someone feels intense pleasure or fear or desire, he suffers from them no evil so great as the ones a person might think of, such as falling ill or spending some of his money because of his desires. What he suffers is the greatest and most extreme of all evils, and he does not take it into his reckoning.
What is that, Socrates? said Cebes.

That the soul of every human being, when it feels intense pleasure or pain at something, is forced at the same moment to believe that the thing it feels this about most strongly is the clearest and truest thing, when it is not so. And these are above all the visible things. Is that not so?
Certainly.
And is it not in this experience that soul is most tightly bound by body?
How so?

Because each pleasure and pain, as if it had a nail, nails the soul to the body and pins it there and makes it bodily, so that it believes that whatever the body says is true. For from sharing the body's beliefs and enjoying the same things it is forced, I think, to become like it in its ways and in its nurture, and to be the kind of soul that never arrives in Hades pure, but always goes out full of the body; so that it soon falls back into another body and grows in it as if it had been sown, and so has no share in the company of the divine and pure and of one form.
That's most true, Socrates, said Cebes.
It is for these reasons, then, Cebes, that those who are justly lovers of learning are orderly and brave, and not for the reasons the many give. Or do you think it is?
Of course not.

No indeed. The soul of a man who is a philosopher would reason in this way. It would not think that philosophy ought to release it and that, while philosophy is releasing it, it should hand itself over to pleasures and pains to bind it fast again, and so do work that is never done, like some Penelope handling her web the opposite way. Instead it secures a calm from these things, follows reasoning and stays always within it, gazes on what is true and divine and not a matter of belief, and is nourished by that. It thinks that it must live this way for as long as it lives, and that when it dies it will arrive at what is akin to it and of the same kind, and be rid of human evils. After a nurture like that, Simmias and Cebes, there is no danger that it will be afraid of being torn apart at its parting from the body, blown apart by the winds, flying off and gone, and of no longer being anything anywhere.

divergences.phrase: εἰς τοιοῦτον τόπον ἕτερον … ἀιδῆ, εἰς Ἅιδου ὡς ἀληθῶς, παρὰ τὸν ἀγαθὸν καὶ φρόνιμον θεόν
divergences.older: to the place of the true Hades, which like her is invisible, and pure, and noble, and on her way to the good and wise God
divergences.lectio: to another place of that kind, noble and pure and unseen, to Hades, rightly so named, to the good and wise god
divergences.note: In Greek the name Hades sounds like the word for unseen, and Socrates says the soul goes to the place that truly deserves the name. The edition keeps the same word, unseen, on both sides of the name so the play can be heard, and prints the god where Jowett has God: the god meant is Hades.

divergences.phrase: χαριέντως ἔχων τὸ σῶμα … καὶ ἐν τοιαύτῃ ὥρᾳ
divergences.older: if the constitution be sound at the time of death, and the season of the year favourable
divergences.lectio: with his body in fine condition and in a season as fine
divergences.note: The Greek word can mean a season of the year or the bloom of a person's life, and Burnet took it the second way. The edition leaves the word as open as Plato left it.

divergences.phrase: ὡς ἂν μάλιστα αὐτὸς ὁ δεδεμένος συλλήπτωρ εἴη τοῦ δεδέσθαι
divergences.older: by reason of lust had become the principal accomplice in her own captivity
divergences.lectio: so that the prisoner himself is the chief accomplice in his own imprisonment
divergences.note: Jowett rearranges the long sentence and makes it a history of the soul. In the Greek it is what philosophy sees when it looks at the prison: the bars are desire, so the one locked in helps to lock himself in. The edition keeps Plato's order, including his breaking off and starting again.
